statements.quote: This first statistics chapter introduces the mathematical framework for reasoning under uncertainty.
The core idea: real-world data is not random noise; it follows **distributions** that we can model, sample from, and use to make decisions.
By the end, you will recognize the key distributions (Normal, Bernoulli, Binomial, Chi-Square, Zipf) and understand how **statistical inference** lets us draw conclusions from samples.
Artificial Intelligence is often described as “Applied Statistics”: at its core, every decision an AI makes is a calculation of likelihoods.
The frameworks below come from diverse origins — games of chance, mapping the heavens — and now enable machines to learn from data.
\citetitle{flammarion}: A symbol of the drive to venture beyond the limits of current understanding
The goal of studying distributions is not to memorize them, but to understand how large datasets behave.

blocks.quote: This first statistics chapter introduces the mathematical framework for reasoning under uncertainty. The core idea: real-world data is not random noise; it follows **distributions** that we can model, sample from, and use to make decisions.
By the end, you will recognize the key distributions (Normal, Bernoulli, Binomial, Chi-Square, Zipf) and understand how **statistical inference** lets us draw conclusions from samples.

Artificial Intelligence is often described as “Applied Statistics”: at its core, every decision an AI makes is a calculation of likelihoods. The frameworks below come from diverse origins — games of chance, mapping the heavens — and now enable machines to learn from data.
\citetitle{flammarion}: A symbol of the drive to venture beyond the limits of current understanding
Distributions
blocks.section: Distributions

blocks.quote: The goal of studying distributions is not to memorize them, but to understand how large datasets behave. Real-world data rarely matches a theoretical distribution perfectly, but studying the distributions changes how you see the data: not as isolated points, but as a cohesive whole.
blocks.section: Distributions

blocks.quote: In practice, many real-world datasets approximate a theoretical distribution closely enough for the model to be useful, and the statistical methods applied to them remain reliable even when the match is imperfect.
blocks.section: Distributions

blocks.quote: Methods used here are also applied in many areas of Machine Learning, such as **initializing neural networks**, **generating synthetic data**, **modeling uncertainty in predictions**, and **optimizing algorithms**. Understanding distributions is a foundational skill that bridges statistical theory and practical applications in AI and data science.
blocks.section: Distributions

blocks.quote: How knowing about distributions helps in developing AI systems
blocks.section: How knowing about distributions helps in developing AI systems

blocks.quote: Recognizing these distributions in real-world data — from telescope photons to pixel intensities in medical imaging — lets machines model uncertainty. Most natural phenomena are not random noise but follow mathematical patterns; by recognizing a Gaussian distribution, an AI can separate meaningful “signal” from background noise. For example, in autonomous driving, a sensor must decide whether a blurred shape is a pedestrian or a lens flare. Knowing the distribution of typical sensor errors lets the machine make a calculated “guess” rather than stalling on an exact match: abstracting the data into a probability curve is the “extra level of indirection” that, as David Wheeler is credited with saying, can solve any problem.
blocks.section: How knowing about distributions helps in developing AI systems

blocks.quote: These distributions also underpin the “scaling laws” that drive modern large language models. As described in \citetitle{sutton2019bitter} by Rich Sutton, progress in AI comes from “general methods that leverage computation” rather than hand-coded human knowledge. When an AI is trained on vast datasets, it is essentially learning to map the distribution of human language; applications like predictive text and weather forecasting rely on the fact that the next word or the next storm front follows a predictable frequency distribution. Knowing these patterns lets developers make choices — from initializing neural networks to selecting training data — that match the variation actually present in the data.
blocks.section: How knowing about distributions helps in developing AI systems

blocks.quote: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
blocks.section: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT)

blocks.quote: The **Central Limit Theorem** is the bridge between randomness and order. It explains why, even when individual events are chaotic or “flat,” their collective averages inevitably form the **Normal Distribution** (the “Bell Curve”). De Moivre first proved the binomial case in the 1730s; \citeauthor{laplace1810clt} generalized it to sums of independent variables in \citeyear{laplace1810clt}.
blocks.section: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT)

blocks.quote: The first version of the CLT came out of the eighteenth-century analysis of games of chance; **\citeauthor{laplace1810clt}** generalized it in \citeyear{laplace1810clt}, in the context of the “Problem of Errors” in astronomy.
blocks.section: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT)

blocks.quote: Astronomers of the era faced a dilemma: every measurement taken via telescope or pendulum was slightly “noisy” due to atmospheric disturbances or human imperfection. Laplace proved that the **average** of these independent errors follows a bell curve, whatever the shape of the individual error distribution, provided its variance is finite. By aggregating many imprecise data points, one can mathematically “filter” the noise to recover the true position of a celestial body — a method that remains the foundation for how machines learn from “imperfect” real-world data.

blocks.quote: Statistics as a state technique: from mortality tables to the average man
blocks.section: Statistics as a state technique: from mortality tables to the average man

blocks.quote: Before statistics was a neutral tool in a mathematician's hand, it was an instrument of the **state** — a way to know a population well enough to tax it, mobilize it, and govern it. Its origins are less mathematical than you might expect.
blocks.section: Statistics as a state technique: from mortality tables to the average man

blocks.quote: The first step was to *count* people. In 1662, the London haberdasher John Graunt took the city's weekly Bills of Mortality — the death records the churches kept for burial fees — and turned them into a model. From a handful of parish records he estimated the size of the whole city, separated plague deaths from ordinary causes, and built what we would now call a **life table**: the probability of surviving to each age \cite[Graunt, *Bills of Mortality* (1662)]{graunt1662}. This was the birth of **demography**, then known as *political arithmetic* — using numbers to understand a political body, not a probability.
blocks.section: Statistics as a state technique: from mortality tables to the average man

blocks.quote: \marginfig{john_graunt.png}{John Graunt (1620–1674), father of demography. Public domain (book illustration).}
blocks.section: Statistics as a state technique: from mortality tables to the average man

blocks.quote: The second step was to find the *average*. \citeauthor{quetelet1835} (\citeyear{quetelet1835}), a Belgian astronomer turned statistician, argued that human behavior obeys **social physics** as surely as weather does: crime rates, marriage ages, even suicide counts fluctuate around a stable mean. His device was the **l'homme moyen**, the *average man* — a hypothetical person defined by the mean value of every measured trait \cite[Quetelet, *social physics* (1835)]{quetelet1835}. The average man was a **model of the population**, and once you have one, you can sort everyone by their deviation from it. (That machinery now underlies every "typical user" assumption and every outlier-detection step in a data pipeline.)
blocks.section: Statistics as a state technique: from mortality tables to the average man

blocks.quote: \marginfig{adolphe_quetelet.jpg}{Adolphe Quetelet (1796–1874), inventor of the "average man". Public domain (Demannez engraving).}
blocks.section: Statistics as a state technique: from mortality tables to the average man

blocks.quote: Here is the part most textbooks skip. The man who carried the average-man idea into its most consequential — and most troubling — application was \cite[Francis Galton]{galton_eugenics}, and the data that produced your linear regression was a question of *breeding*. Galton, an inventor, an explorer, and Darwin's cousin, asked how strongly traits like height are **passed from parent to child**. Measuring hundreds of families, he found that tall parents' children tend to be shorter than them, and short parents' taller: offspring **regress toward the mean** \cite[regression to the mean, from Galton's height data]{galton}. He coined the word **eugenics** in 1883, and he built this machinery to study hereditary variation with the explicit aim of *improving* — and later *controlling* — the human stock \cite[Francis Galton (eugenics)]{galton_eugenics}. Linear regression was, in origin, a tool for measuring the transmission of traits across generations.
blocks.section: Statistics as a state technique: from mortality tables to the average man

blocks.quote: \marginfig{sir_francis_galton.jpg}{Francis Galton (1822–1911): origin of regression — and of eugenics. Public domain (Oakley, NPG).}
blocks.section: Statistics as a state technique: from mortality tables to the average man

blocks.quote: That history does not invalidate the mathematics — least squares is least squares regardless of who first applied it — but it belongs in the prehistory, not a footnote: **statistics was invented, in part, as a state technique for ranking populations**. The next section is that same data in Pearson's hands: parent-and-child heights, turned into a correlation coefficient.

blocks.quote: The t-Test: A Dublin Brewery's Answer to Small Samples
blocks.section: The t-Test: A Dublin Brewery's Answer to Small Samples

blocks.quote: You now hold both ingredients — a standard Normal in the numerator, a $\chi^2$ in the denominator — for the most-used significance test in science. Its origin is one of the strangest in the history of statistics: not a university, but an Irish **brewery**.
blocks.section: The t-Test: A Dublin Brewery's Answer to Small Samples

blocks.quote: In \citeyear{student1908probableerror}, the journal *Biometrika* published "The Probable Error of a Mean" under the pseudonym **"Student"** \cite{student1908probableerror}. The author was **William Sealy Gosset** (1876–1937), a chemist who joined the Arthur Guinness & Son brewery in Dublin in 1899 and spent his whole career there \cite{pearson1990studentbio}. Guinness was the world's largest brewery, and its quality control had grown beyond the eye and the nose: to judge a shipment of barley, malt, or hops from a **small sample** — testing the whole harvest was too costly and too destructive. In an internal report from 1904 he noticed that the usual "law of error" machinery was unreliable with only a handful of observations, and in 1906–07 the company sent him for two terms to **Karl Pearson's** Biometric Laboratory in London \cite{studentstest_wiki}.
blocks.section: The t-Test: A Dublin Brewery's Answer to Small Samples

blocks.quote: The pseudonym had a commercial reason: after one of the lab's papers revealed details that might serve competitors, Guinness forbade its staff from mentioning beer, the brewery, or their real names in print \cite{ziliak2008guinnessometrics}. The method therefore carried a false name for a century. It stayed obscure until **Ronald Fisher** — whom Gosset corresponded with in more than 150 letters between 1912 and 1934 — recognized what he had done: in a 1912 letter he pointed out that the scaling should use degrees of freedom, the corrected **Student's t** tables appeared in a 1925 special issue of *Metron*, and Fisher's applications of the test to regression appeared in the same volume \cite{studentstest_wiki}. Fisher called it a "logical revolution"; Gosset's dry reply to an admirer was: "Fisher would have discovered it all anyway." The brewery's barley trials also seeded the field's first great design debate — Gosset's **balanced** layouts (matching plots by soil and climate) against Fisher's **randomization**, a rivalry that shaped experimental design for decades \cite{ziliak2008guinnessometrics}.
blocks.section: The t-Test: A Dublin Brewery's Answer to Small Samples

blocks.quote: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation
blocks.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

blocks.quote: Testing a difference is only half the discipline. The other half — the one that actually *creates* trustworthy evidence — is **designing an experiment** that produces a difference you can trust. That design was invented in three stages, and each is a direct ancestor of something you do in ML.
blocks.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

blocks.quote: The first stage was the **control group**. In 1747, the Royal Navy surgeon James Lind split twelve scorbutic sailors on the warship *Salisbury* into pairs, each pair given a different treatment — one pair took two oranges and a lemon a day. Within days, one of them was fit for duty and the other "almost recovered"; the pair on cider also improved, but the four other pairs — vitriol, vinegar, sea-water, and a balsam-of-Peru/garlic/myrrh/mustard/radish mixture — showed no improvement at all \cite[Lind, *A Treatise of the Scurvy* (1753)]{lind1747scurvy} \cite{scurvy_wiki}. Nobody *proved* citrus cured scurvy (the sample was tiny), but the **design** — pair the patients, give different treatments, compare — is the exact shape of a control group.
blocks.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

blocks.quote: \marginfig{james_lind.jpg}{James Lind (1716–1794), whose 1747 scurvy trial was among the first controlled trials. Public domain (Chalmers, 1783).}
blocks.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

blocks.quote: The second stage, and the one that matters most, was **randomization**, and it came from \cite[Ronald Fisher, *The Design of Experiments* (1935)]{fisher1935design}. The problem Lind faced but could not fully solve: even with pairs, the two patients might differ in age, diet, or constitution, so *who* receives which treatment leaks into the comparison. Fisher's answer was to **assign treatments by chance**. Randomization does not remove hidden confounders; it *distributes* them across the groups on average, so the only systematic difference between the groups is the treatment itself. The book gave the null hypothesis its canonical exposition; randomization had already appeared in *Statistical Methods for Research Workers* (1925) and "The Arrangement of Field Experiments" (1926), and replication and factorial design were not new in 1935 (\cite{design_of_experiments_wiki}).
blocks.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

blocks.quote: The third stage was the **double-blind** procedure: neither the person giving the treatment nor the one receiving it knows who is in the control group, so that expectation — the experimenter's *or* the subject's — cannot tint the result \cite[the double-blind study]{doubleblind}. It matured alongside the first large **randomized controlled trials**, the 1948 streptomycin studies that set the template for medical evidence \cite[randomized controlled trial]{rct1948}.
blocks.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation

blocks.quote: Now map it onto what you do. An **A/B test** — ship variant A of a page to half your users, variant B to the other half, compare the metric — is Fisher's randomization applied to software. And an **ablation study** — remove one component of the model and measure what the metric does — is Lind's control group applied to architecture: the full model is the control, the ablated model is the "treatment", and the question *is the drop from removing this layer real, or noise?* is answered by the t-test from the last section. The whole discipline of judging a model by **deliberately breaking it and measuring** descends, step for step, from a surgeon pairing up scurvy sailors on a warship.
blocks.section: The controlled experiment: from scurvy to ablation
